abstract: Human and ape genomes contain regions enriched in interspersed segmental duplications (SDs) that promote gene innovation and predispose to pathogenic rearrangements. Mechanisms driving SD expansion in the human genome remain poorly understood, although SDs cluster around high-copy ancestral core duplicons and exhibit Alu enrichment at their boundaries. Here, we investigate structural diversity and evolution at the disease-associated 16p12.3-p13.11 locus, comprising four SD clusters organized around the LCR16a core duplicon. Analysis of 94 haploid human genomes reveals 12 alternative structural configurations across clusters 1-2 and eight across clusters 3-4, with different predicted susceptibilities to pathogenic rearrangements. These include two deletions and four inversions arising through nonallelic homologous recombination (NAHR) or nonhomologous end joining. We identify two types of multiallelic tandem duplications involving LCR16a and an adjacent segment, both arising through Alu-Alu NAHR. We characterize two complex insertions whose structures and breakpoint features support models involving double template switching, preferentially involving homologous sites within LCR16a duplicons (empirical p = 3 x 10-4) and/or Alu elements (empirical p = 0.029). Evolutionary analyses suggest that clusters 3 and 4 expanded approximately 6 million years ago in the human-chimpanzee common ancestor through double template switching involving Alu repeats. Clusters 1 and 2 expanded through two human-specific duplicative transpositions, possibly mediated by circular DNA intermediates, with LCR16a sequences at both reintegration breakpoints and insertion sites, generating the human-specific NOMO1 gene. These findings implicate Alu elements and LCR16a duplicons in SD formation and genomic instability at 16p12.3-p13.11 through recombination-, replication-, and circular DNA-based mechanisms.
